narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimated a 64% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, failure was judged more likely than success, and that risk was treated as too high for admission.

The strongest factor pushing toward failure was your plan to study part-time rather than full-time. Among accepted students, about 92.8% were full-time, so your part-time status was the single largest concern. The second most influential factor was your third-year class standing: your standing of 7 was above the accepted-student average of about 5.8, so this factor worked in your favor and pushed toward passing. It was not enough, however, to outweigh the other concerns. The third most important factor was your first-year class standing: your standing of 4 was below the accepted-student average of 6, so it pushed toward failure. Your LSAT score of 37 and undergraduate GPA of 3.20 were close to accepted-student averages, so they did not materially change the overall picture.

To improve a future application, consider whether a full-time study plan is feasible, and show stronger early academic performance or a clear upward trend. You may also strengthen your LSAT preparation and seek admissions counseling before reapplying.
